Part B · Chapter 7

Fine-tuning, forgetting and continual learning

Why fine-tuning on a new water can make a model forget the old one, and how springs on its weights can limit that

Fine-tuning SharkCam on murky-water dives can lower its accuracy in the clear water it knew. This chapter covers brakes on overfitting, pretraining, catastrophic forgetting, the Fisher information, elastic weight consolidation, Adam's v as a Fisher proxy (the idea behind my optimizer-state work), continual learning and test-time training. The figures use small PyTorch models on made-up spadenose records. A "water" is a made-up change in the robot's length and clarity readings.

You will need: mini-batches (B3), Adam's \(m\) and \(v\) and its first look at curvature (B5), dropout (B6), overfitting and validation sets (A4), curvature (0.6) and expectation (0.7).

Four waters, one question

Guess first. SharkCam learned in clear water to call a spadenose shark "mature" when its length is above about 34 cm. In murky water the camera reads all sharks 38% too short. About how many of 108 test sharks does this clear-water rule get right: about 90%, about 60% or about 35%?

The camera reports the apparent length, the true length \(L\) times a factor \(f\) that depends on the water. The clear-water rule says "mature" when the apparent length is above a cut of 34.25 cm, which is the same as testing whether \(L\) is above \(34.25/f\). When \(f\) falls, a shark must be longer to exceed the cut, so the rule calls more mature sharks immature. A task is one version of the problem, here one water. The factors are made up.

  1. Blue dots are immature and coral diamonds mature sharks, placed by the length the camera reads; the dashed line is the cut. Choose Murky water: the dots move left, and most end left of the line, so the share right in the readout falls from 87% to 36%.
  2. The teal line is the cut that would give the clear-water answers again. It moves with the dots, to 21.2 cm (62% of 34.25 cm) in murky water.

In clear, hazy and murky water the clear-water rule is right for 87%, 64% and 36% of the 108 test sharks, so the answer to the guess is about 35%.

How it works

Take murky water, where \(f = 0.62\). The rule calls a shark mature when \(0.62 \times L\) is above 34.25 cm, so \(L\) must be above \(34.25/0.62 = 55.2\) cm. Of the 108 test sharks, 72 are mature and 36 are immature. Only 3 are longer than 55.2 cm, and all 3 are mature. The rule calls the other 105 immature, so it is right for these 3 and for all 36 immature ones: 39 of 108, or 36%.

34.25 cmcut on the apparent length÷\(f\) = 0.62factor of murky water=55.2 cmtrue length \(L\) a shark needs→39 of 108right: 36%

Common belief. A rule that is right for 87% of the test sharks stays about as accurate in new conditions.

Why it fails. The 108 test sharks are the same in all four waters (clear, hazy, murky and monsoon silt). Only the readings change, and the clear-water rule is right for 64% in hazy water and 36% in murky water.

Better account. A test result describes a rule for the kind of readings it was tested on. After the water changes, test the rule again on labelled sharks from the new water.

Quick quiz

In murky water the camera reads 62% of the true length. What does it read for Tag 3305, a 41.0 cm mature spadenose, and does the clear-water rule still call it mature?

\(0.62 \times 41.0 = 25.4\) cm. That is below the 34.25 cm cut, so the rule calls it immature, which is wrong.

In hazy water \(f = 0.80\). How long must a spadenose be for the clear-water rule to call it mature, and how many test sharks does the rule get right?

\(34.25/0.80 = 42.8\) cm. In hazy water the rule is right for 69 of the 108 test sharks, which is 64%.

Go deeper the other waters, a clarity sensor, Python about 4 min

The clarity sensor

The made-up factors 1.00, 0.62, 0.80 and 0.48 are our own choice, exaggerated so that the effect is clear. They are not measurements. In the story, haze in murky water hides the tail, so the camera reads sharks shorter. The sharks did not change, only the readings, and a model trained in clear water has no input that says the water changed. That is why the made-up robot has a clarity sensor, which reports the water's visibility in metres, and feeds this clarity reading to the network as a fourth input next to length, girth and depth. In clear water the reading is about 8 m for all training sharks, so it has no information there. It becomes useful only after other waters arrive. The figures add a small made-up noise of 0.4 m to the readings, as a physical sensor would have.

The other waters

The same arithmetic gives the other waters. In hazy water (\(f = 0.80\)) the threshold is \(34.25/0.80 = 42.8\) cm, 33 of the 108 test sharks reach it, and the rule is right for 69 of 108, or 64%. In silt (\(f = 0.48\)) the threshold is 71.4 cm. The longest spadenose in the made-up table is 59.8 cm, so the rule calls all the sharks immature and is right for the immature share, 36 of 108 or 33%.

34.25 ÷ 0.80hazy water=42.8 cm33 sharks pass, 64% right|34.25 ÷ 0.62murky water=55.2 cm3 pass, 36% right|34.25 ÷ 0.48silt=71.4 cmnone pass, 33% right

In Python

import json, numpy as np

rec = [r for r in json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"] if r["species"] == "spadenose"]
L = np.array([r["length_cm"] for r in rec]); mature = np.array([r["mature"] for r in rec])
test = np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(len(rec))[160:]       # the 108 test sharks of the figures
cut = 34.25                                                       # the clear-water rule: "mature" above this reading

print("water   factor  true length needed  sharks that pass  right")
for name, f in [("clear", 1.00), ("hazy", 0.80), ("murky", 0.62), ("silt", 0.48)]:
    called_mature = f * L[test] > cut                             # what the rule says, given the camera's reading
    right = (called_mature == (mature[test] == 1)).sum()
    print("%-7s %.2f    %6.2f cm          %3d               %3d of 108 (%.0f%%)" % (
          name, f, cut / f, called_mature.sum(), right, 100 * right / 108))
water   factor  true length needed  sharks that pass  right
clear   1.00     34.25 cm           76                94 of 108 (87%)
hazy    0.80     42.81 cm           33                69 of 108 (64%)
murky   0.62     55.24 cm            3                39 of 108 (36%)
silt    0.48     71.35 cm            0                36 of 108 (33%)

The table repeats the figure's numbers, and shows that only the factor moves.

In practice

The repair is to move the cut with the water. In murky water the cut becomes \(34.25 \times 0.62 = 21.2\) cm in the readings, the same shark length as 34.25 cm in clear water. That needs \(f\), which the rule cannot learn from the readings alone. A camera could measure it from an object of known size in view. If a 30 cm marker on the robot's arm (a made-up detail of the story) reads 18.6 cm, then \(f = 18.6/30 = 0.62\). Without such a reference the robot needs labelled sharks from the new water, which is the subject of the next sections.

The model used in the rest of the chapter

The model in the rest of the chapter is small. A logistic regression has the weights \(w\) (on length), \(b\) (the bias) and \(c\) (on the clarity reading). Its weighted sum is \(z = w\,x + b + c\,v\), with \(x\) the standardised apparent length and \(v\) the standardised clarity. The small network has four inputs, four hidden ReLU units and one output: \(4\times4 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 25\) weights. Both use the log loss of A3 and B3. Four waters arrive in this order: clear (8 m), murky (2 m, factor 0.62), hazy (4 m, factor 0.80) and silt (1 m, factor 0.48).

More questions

Why is the clarity reading useless in the first water?

It has almost the same value for all training sharks, so changing its weight changes all predictions in nearly the same way as the bias does. The training sharks can hardly tell the two apart, and the reading does not predict maturity.

Brakes on overfitting: a penalty, early stopping and noise

Guess first. A network with 1,300 weights trains on only 30 sharks, and its training loss falls toward 0. What does its validation loss, measured on held-out sharks, do: keep falling, stop changing, or start rising?

A network with more weights than examples can fit the noise (random variation that does not repeat in new sharks) in 30 made-up sharks as well as what they have in common. Regularisation, a brake on overfitting, is any method that stops the fit from following the noise. A weight penalty adds a term to the loss that grows with the size of the weights. Early stopping ends training when the validation loss stops improving. Noise in the inputs is data augmentation, training on altered copies: it adds small random amounts to the 30 sharks at the start of an epoch, one pass over them.

  1. With penalty and noise both on none, the navy training loss falls to 0.00. The coral validation loss, checked at epochs 4, 8, 12 and on, is lowest at epoch 12 (teal dotted line) and then climbs. With patience 3 (stop after 3 checks without a new lowest value), training stops at epoch 24 (grey dashed line).
  2. Choose a weight penalty of 0.05, or input noise of 0.6 with no penalty, and watch where the validation loss ends.

With no brake the validation loss climbs from 0.36 at epoch 12 to 2.03 at epoch 400, while a weight penalty of 0.05 or input noise of 0.6 ends at 0.35 or 0.46.

How it works

Early stopping by hand. With no brake the checks at epochs 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 read 0.56, 0.42, 0.36, 0.40, 0.50 and 0.63. With patience 3, the checks at epochs 16, 20 and 24 give no new lowest value, so training stops at epoch 24 and the run keeps the weights of epoch 12.

A weight penalty by hand. The loss becomes \(L_{\text{total}} = L + \omega\sum_j\theta_j^2\), where \(L\) is the loss on the training data, \(\sum_j\) adds over the weights \(\theta_j\), and \(\omega\) is a strength that a person chooses. The penalty's slope is \(2\omega\theta_j\), so a plain gradient step with learning rate \(\eta\) also shrinks all weights by the factor \(1-2\eta\omega\).

0.05ω, the penalty strength×93², a weight of 3 squared=0.45added to the loss|1 − 2 × 0.1 × 0.05η = 0.1=0.99weights shrink 1% per step

Common belief. A model that fits the training data perfectly is a better model.

Why it fails. At epoch 400 the training loss is 0.00, yet the validation loss is 2.03, almost six times its lowest value, 0.36.

Better account. A widening gap between the curves signals overfitting. A brake is worth keeping if it shrinks the gap without raising the validation loss.

Quick quiz

With \(\omega = 0.05\) and \(\eta = 0.1\), by what factor does a weight shrink in one step if the loss slope is 0?

\(1 - 2 \times 0.1 \times 0.05 = 0.99\). After 100 steps, \(0.99^{100} = 0.37\) of the weight is left.

The validation losses at six checks are 0.50, 0.41, 0.38, 0.39, 0.40 and 0.42, and the patience is 2. When does the run stop, and which weights does the run keep?

The best value, 0.38, comes at check 3. Checks 4 and 5 give no new best, so the run stops at check 5 and keeps the weights of check 3.

Go deeper step by step, noise, Python, where brakes fail about 5 min

Why the validation loss turns

After about 12 epochs the network has probably learned what is common to all sharks and starts to memorise the 30 it sees: the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss rises. Large weights are usually what a network needs to bend a curve through noisy points, so a weight penalty tends to keep the curve smooth. The shrinking of all weights by the factor \(1 - 2\eta\omega\) at a step is why people call it weight decay. B5 explains why Adam treats it differently from a plain penalty. Early stopping needs no change to the loss. Check the validation loss at regular intervals, remember the best weights, and stop when there has been no new best for the patience you set. A network usually starts with small weights and they grow as training goes on, so stopping early tends to keep them small, as a penalty does.

Noise in the inputs

Noise in the inputs is a simple case of data augmentation (C3 develops it for images). At the start of an epoch, all inputs are changed by random amounts of the size you choose (in standardised units, so 0.3 is 30% of a standard deviation). The network never sees the same 30 numbers twice, so memorising them is harder. For a single linear model with squared error, noise of size \(s\) on an input acts like a penalty \(s^2 w^2\) on its weight (exercise 2). This links the first and third brake.

The penalty as an equation

\[ L_{\text{total}}(\theta) \;=\; L(\theta) \;+\; \omega \sum_j \theta_j^{2} \qquad\quad \theta_j \;\leftarrow\; (1 - 2\eta\omega)\,\theta_j \;-\; \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_j} \]

  • \(L\) is the loss on the training data and \(\omega\) (omega) is the penalty strength, a number you choose. B5 uses the same letter, and \(\lambda\) is kept for the EWC strength below.
  • \(\theta_j\) is one weight and \(\eta\) the learning rate. The second form is the first one differentiated: the penalty's slope is \(2\omega\theta_j\), which pulls a weight toward 0.

A penalty, step by step

Take a weight of 3, with \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(\omega = 0.05\). If the loss slope is 0.15, the step gives \(0.99 \times 3 - 0.1 \times 0.15 = 2.955\), and both parts push the weight down. If the loss slope is \(-0.30\), the step gives \(2.97 + 0.03 = 3.00\) and the weight stays. So a penalty of 0.05 lets a weight of 3 keep its size only if the loss slope is \(-0.30\). That is the size of \(2\omega w\). Strength matters. After 400 epochs the validation loss is 2.03 with no penalty, 0.90 with \(\omega = 0.001\), 0.51 with 0.01 and 0.35 with 0.05. The strongest penalty ends close to the best value that early stopping finds, 0.36. The two brakes reach one loss by different routes.

In Python

Input noise can be checked against the penalty in a short script, in the spirit of exercise 2. The noise has size \(s = 0.6\) standard deviations on the standardised length of 30 sharks.

import json, numpy as np

rec = [r for r in json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"] if r["species"] == "spadenose"][:30]
x = np.array([r["length_cm"] for r in rec]); y = np.array([r["mature"] for r in rec], float)
x = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()            # standardised length, mean 0
y = y - y.mean()                        # centred maturity, so no bias term is needed
m, s = len(x), 0.6                      # 30 sharks, noise of 0.6 standard deviations

w_plain = (x @ y) / (x @ x)             # least squares, no brake
w_ridge = (x @ y) / (x @ x + m * s**2)  # the same fit with a weight penalty omega = s squared

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
copies = np.tile(x, 4000) + s * rng.standard_normal(m * 4000)    # 4,000 noisy copies of the 30 sharks
w_noise = (copies @ np.tile(y, 4000)) / (copies @ copies)         # least squares on the noisy copies

print("no brake          w = %.3f" % w_plain)
print("penalty %.2f      w = %.3f" % (s**2, w_ridge))
print("input noise %.1f   w = %.3f" % (s, w_noise))
print("shrink factor 1 / (1 + s^2) = %.3f, and %.3f / %.3f = %.3f" % (1 / (1 + s**2), w_ridge, w_plain, w_ridge / w_plain))
no brake          w = 0.309
penalty 0.36      w = 0.227
input noise 0.6   w = 0.226
shrink factor 1 / (1 + s^2) = 0.735, and 0.227 / 0.309 = 0.735

For a straight-line fit with squared error, noise of size \(s\) shrinks the fitted weight by the same factor as a penalty \(\omega = s^2\). For a standardised input that factor is \(1/(1+s^2)\), here 0.735, and both routes give a weight of 0.226 or 0.227 against 0.309 with no brake. The match is close and not complete, because a finite number of noisy copies is a sample.

Where the brakes fail

Augmentation helps when the altered copies are still correct examples. Try a different alteration: multiply a shark's length, girth and weight by a random factor up to 25% and keep its label. In a test run (10 networks) this lowered the clear-water validation accuracy from 82.1% to 78.8%, and a likely reason is that a shark that is 25% longer may no longer have the same maturity. The augmentation has to mirror a variation that does not change the answer. Early stopping can also stop too soon if the validation set is small and noisy (A4 gives the interval for 108 sharks). In practice, people use all three at once: a small penalty (\(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-2}\) is common), a patience of a few epochs, and an augmentation that matches the data. A frequent mistake is to pick the stopping epoch with the test set. Use the validation set, as in A4.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the validation loss is lowest at epoch 1 or 2, the learning rate is probably too high, so the run overfits within a few steps. Lower the rate before adding brakes (B8).

More questions

Early stopping with patience 3 never fires in a run. What does the figure say about the run?

The validation loss keeps reaching new lows. The run is not overfitting yet, so training for longer is allowed.

How the figure was made

The curves are means of 6 runs on the made-up spadenose records (30 training sharks, 108 validation sharks, six inputs including depth and month, which have no information about maturity). With no brake the training loss reaches 0.00.

Pretraining and fine-tuning

Guess first. A network trained in clear water now gets only 4 labelled sharks from the murky water. Is it better to train it further on those 4, or to start a new network on those 4? And what happens to its accuracy in clear water?

Pretraining is training on an earlier task, here the clear water, so that the weights start in a useful place. Fine-tuning continues training from those weights on the new task. It can train all weights or only the last layer, which freezes (keeps fixed) the other weights. Training from scratch starts from random weights instead.

  1. The slider starts at 4 labelled murky-water sharks (made-up records). In the murky-water view (means of 20 networks), training from scratch (navy) is right for 67% of the 108 test sharks, fine-tuning all weights (teal) for 73% and training only the last layer (sand) for 75%. The pretrained network with no further training (dashed) is right for 38%.
  2. Drag the slider to 16 and then to 160 sharks: the scratch and fine-tuning curves meet, with a gap under 1 point.
  3. Choose accuracy back in clear water: the two pretrained curves, teal and sand, fall from the dashed 88% to between 70% and 74%.

With 4 murky-water sharks, training only the last layer is right for 75%, fine-tuning all weights for 73% and training from scratch for 67%; by 16 sharks fine-tuning has lowered clear-water accuracy from 88% to 72%.

How it works

Count the free weights. The network has 4 inputs (length, girth, depth and clarity reading), 4 hidden units and 1 output, so it has 25 weights, and the output layer alone has 5. A bias is a weight whose input is always 1. With only 4 labelled sharks, 25 free weights are more than 6 per shark (25/4 = 6.25), and many settings of them match all 4 labels. Fine-tuning begins at the weights that fitted the clear water, a likely reason why it beats a random start when labelled sharks are few. In this example, fine-tuning beat training from scratch by 5 and 6 points at 2 and 4 labelled sharks and matched it within 1 point from 8 sharks on. It also lowered clear-water accuracy.

4 × 4inputs to hidden units+4hidden biases+4hidden units to output+1output bias=25weights, 5 in the output layer

Common belief. Fine-tuning adds the new skill to the old one.

Why it fails. Fine-tuning changes the same weights that produced the old predictions, so the old predictions change too. In the figure, fine-tuning on 16 sharks gives 82% in murky water, but clear-water accuracy falls from 88% to 72%.

Better account. Fine-tuning can raise accuracy in the new water and lower it in the old water. Check the old water too, and compare with a network trained from scratch on the same new data.

Quick quiz

With 4 murky-water sharks, which of the three runs is most accurate in murky water, and what happens to its clear-water accuracy?

Training only the last layer, which is right for 75% of the test sharks. In the clear-water view its accuracy falls from 88% to 70%.

Training only the 5 output weights beats training all 25 at 2 and 4 sharks and loses from 8 sharks on. Why?

A likely reason is that 2 to 4 sharks are too little data to adjust 25 weights safely, so changing only the 5 output weights overfits less. With 8 or more sharks the early layers also need to move, and the frozen ones limit the model.

Go deeper reading the figure, the learning rate, Python about 5 min

Reading the clear-water view

The clear-water view shows the cost of fine-tuning: accuracy in the old water drops to 70 to 74% whichever way you fine-tune. Freezing the first layer leaves those weights unchanged but does not protect the output weights, which are the only ones that train in that run. A network from scratch has no old skill to lose, because it never trained on the clear water. In this figure it still reaches 81 to 82% in clear water from 16 sharks on, above the fine-tuned networks, and the figure does not show why.

Why fine-tuning helps

A likely reason why fine-tuning helps is where the weights start. A random network has to find weights that read length and girth at all, and the pretrained network already has such weights. Many settings of the 25 weights match 4 labels, so which one training reaches depends on the starting point. This is a likely reason why a pretrained start helps most when data is scarce. In this made-up shift the length readings are only rescaled, so a likely need is a moved threshold rather than new features. Practitioners use the same logic at a large scale. They start from a model pretrained on a large data set. A common choice is a fine-tuning learning rate about ten times smaller than the original, so that the early layers are not wiped out, and the early layers are often frozen. A cheaper variant keeps all weights frozen and trains a small add-on, which my optimizer-state primer describes as LoRA (low-rank adaptation).

The learning rate

The learning rate also matters. The code below fine-tunes 20 clear-water networks for 150 Adam steps at five rates, and prints the means. The 20 networks use different draws of 8 murky-water sharks. The figure's fine-tuning uses 150 steps at rate 0.01. At 0.0003 the first layer moves only 5% of its size, and the murky accuracy rises from 36.5% to just 38.8%. At 0.001 it moves 14%, with murky 50% and clear 85%. At 0.003 it moves 26%, with murky 78% and clear 77%. Above that the murky accuracy stays near 77 or 78% while the first layer moves further, 33% and then 48%, and the clear-water accuracy does not recover (75% and 77%). The clear-water network was trained at 0.02, so the useful rates, 0.003 to 0.01, are 2 to 7 times smaller. A rate that is too small teaches almost none of the new water in 150 steps. A larger one learns the new water and loses the old at the same time.

# uses the set-up lines at the end of the page
bases = []                                                       # 20 clear-water networks, one per seed
for s in range(20):
    torch.manual_seed(s); b = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 1))
    fit(b, XA, 300, seed=s + 1); bases.append(b)

def tune(lr, k=8, steps=150):
    """Fine-tune each network on its own k murky-water sharks; mean over the 20 networks."""
    out = []
    for s, base in enumerate(bases):
        pick = np.random.RandomState(s + 1000).choice(tr, k, replace=False)
        m = copy.deepcopy(base); opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=lr)
        for _ in range(steps):
            opt.zero_grad(); loss_fn(m(XB[pick]).squeeze(1), y[pick]).backward(); opt.step()
        moved = (m[0].weight - base[0].weight).norm() / base[0].weight.norm()        # how far the first layer moved
        out.append([acc(m, XB), acc(m, XA), moved.item()])
    return np.mean(out, 0)

print("no training: murky %.3f  clear %.3f" % (np.mean([acc(b, XB) for b in bases]), np.mean([acc(b, XA) for b in bases])))
print("rate     murky  clear  first layer moved")
for lr in [0.0003, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03]:
    a, b, mv = tune(lr)
    print("%-7g  %.3f  %.3f  %3.0f%% of its size" % (lr, a, b, 100 * mv))
no training: murky 0.365  clear 0.873
rate     murky  clear  first layer moved
0.0003   0.388  0.868    5% of its size
0.001    0.497  0.848   14% of its size
0.003    0.783  0.770   26% of its size
0.01     0.771  0.753   33% of its size
0.03     0.779  0.768   48% of its size

All 20 networks share the same 160 training and 108 test sharks. The figure draws a different split for its 20 networks, so the means differ by a point or two. At 8 sharks and rate 0.01 the figure shows 77% in murky water and 73% in clear water, against 77% and 75% here.

Where it misleads

The benefit disappears as labelled data grows. At 160 sharks, scratch and fine-tuning are about equal at 84 to 85%, and the last-layer-only run is worse (78%), a likely reason being that it cannot change the early layers. Starting from the old weights can also be a poor start: if the new task needs very different features, pretraining may not help. In practice, check three numbers: the new task's validation score, the old task's score, and the score of a network trained from scratch on the same new data.

More questions

Why can fine-tuning be worse than training from scratch when the new task has lots of data?

The old weights are a starting point that may lie in a valley made for the old task. With enough new data, a fresh start can find a valley made for the new task and does not bring the old task's fit along. In the figure the two tie at 160 sharks, so the safe claim is only that the advantage vanishes.

At rate 0.0003 the output shows murky accuracy 38.8% and clear accuracy 86.8%. What did the small rate cost, and what did it buy?

It cost half a point in clear water (87.3% to 86.8%) and bought 2 points in murky water (36.5% to 38.8%). The first layer moved only 5% of its size, so 150 steps barely taught the network the new water. A rate that is too small is safe and does little.

Catastrophic forgetting

Guess first. The network keeps training on murky-water sharks only, for 200 steps. Its murky-water accuracy will climb. What happens to its clear-water accuracy, which it is no longer trained on: stays near 88%, falls by a few points, or falls by 10 points or more?

Catastrophic forgetting is a large drop in accuracy on an old task after training on a new one, when the training data has no examples of the old task. The loss on the murky water has no term for the clear water, so descending it can move the weights anywhere that lowers the new loss. The old optimum \(\theta^*\) is the set of weights at the end of the old training. A move that fits the new water can leave the values that fit the old water.

  1. Press Play: the teal curve (murky water) rises from 38% to 86% while the coral curve (clear water) falls from 88% to 73%. In the readout, the chance of "mature" for Tag 9840, an immature 30.7 cm shark in the made-up table, goes from 0.12 to 0.99.
  2. Drag the scrubber to step 25: clear-water accuracy is already near 70%, and the chance of "mature" for Tag 9840 is 0.97.

Training for 200 steps on murky water raises its accuracy from 38% to 86% and lowers clear-water accuracy from 88% to 73%, a fall of about 15 points.

How it works

Follow Tag 9840, a 30.7 cm immature shark, in a simpler model. The next figure uses a logistic regression with three weights: \(w\) on the standardised length \(x\), the bias \(b\), and \(c\) on \(v\), the standardised clarity reading. Here \(v = (m - 8)/4\) for a visibility of \(m\) metres read by a sensor on the robot. Its weighted sum is \(z = w\,x + b + c\,v\), and the chance of "mature" is \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\). In clear water \(v\) is about 0. For Tag 9840, \(x = (30.7 - 39.14)/8.61 = -0.98\), where 39.14 cm and 8.61 cm are the clear-water mean and spread. At the old optimum (\(w = 5.18\), \(b = 2.94\)), \(z = 5.18 \times (-0.98) + 2.94 = -2.14\), so \(\sigma(-2.14) = 0.105\). With \(w\) held at 5.18, plain fine-tuning moves \(b\) to 11.02, which adds 8.08 to \(z\) for all clear-water sharks, because the input of \(b\) is always 1.

−2.14\(z\) of Tag 9840, old weights+8.08change of \(b\), 11.02 − 2.94=5.94new \(z\)→ σ →0.105 → 0.997chance of "mature"
  1. The plot is a slice of the weight space, which has one axis per weight, so a point is one complete set of weights. The axes are \(b\) and \(c\), and \(w\) stays at its clear-water value. Blue contour lines (lines of equal loss) show the old water's loss and coral lines the new water's.
  2. The navy dot is the old optimum. Follow the dotted coral path of plain fine-tuning to the coral star, 8 units away along \(b\). The readout gives the old water's loss there as 1.76.
  3. Choose no clarity reading: the axes become \(w\) and \(b\), and the old water's loss at the star rises to 2.69.

Common belief. A network that has learned something keeps it, as a saved file keeps its contents.

Why it fails. Weights are shared by all inputs, so training moves them in the direction that helps the current data. Old knowledge is a pattern in these values, and the training step has no term that protects it.

Better account. Plain fine-tuning keeps old knowledge only to the extent that the new loss rewards it. A penalty, stored old examples or frozen weights can protect it too.

Quick quiz

Why does plain fine-tuning end 8 units from the old optimum in \(b\), where it started?

Plain fine-tuning follows the slope of the new loss only, and that loss has no term for the old water. No term in it prefers the point nearest the old optimum, so the path can end far away.

Does forgetting happen if the new data also contains old examples?

Less, because the loss then also rewards the old task. Training on both is the joint-training baseline of a later section, and replay is a cheaper copy of it.

The answer to the guess

The answer to the guess is "falls by 10 points or more": 15 points here, and 18 at the lowest point on the way (70%).

Watching it happen

The code below runs the 200 steps of plain fine-tuning in one network. It prints the two accuracies at steps 0, 25, 50 and on to 200, with the chance of "mature" that the network gives Tag 9840 in clear water. Most of the damage comes in the first 25 steps: clear-water accuracy falls from 86.1% to 77.8% there, and then stays between 77.8% and 80.6%. That spread is 3 sharks out of 108, which is within the noise of one network. The tracked shark moves from 0.18 to 0.67 after 25 steps and ends at 0.79. A check on accuracy alone hides how far single predictions moved.

Reading the weight-space picture

Plain fine-tuning slides from the old optimum (blue dot) to the valley of the new water (coral lines). It ends 8 units away in the bias, where the old water's loss has risen from 0.20 to 1.76. Blue contours are the loss on clear-water sharks and coral contours the loss on murky-water sharks, with the bottom of a valley at the lowest value. The model is the logistic regression with weights \(w\), \(b\) and \(c\).

The two weights are \(b\) (the bias) and \(c\) (the weight on the clarity reading), with \(w\) held at its clear-water value. The blue valley is a vertical band at \(b \approx 2.9\). In clear water the reading is almost the same for all sharks, so \(c\) hardly matters and the loss depends on \(b\) almost alone. The coral valley is a diagonal band. In murky water the reading is \(-1.5\) (standardised), so only the combination \(b - 1.5c\) matters. Many pairs of \((b, c)\) are equally good. Gradient descent starts at the blue dot and follows the slope of the coral loss. In this run it first moves \(b\) and \(c\) together to the coral valley, within about 40 steps, and then drifts along the valley to its lowest point, where \(b\) has changed by a lot. That is the forgetting. Switch to "no clarity reading" to see the harder case: the weights are \(w\) and \(b\), and the two valleys do not overlap at all.

After the shift in b

The shift of 8.08 in the weighted sum raises it for all the immature sharks too, so most of them are called mature and clear-water accuracy falls to 68%, close to the 67% share of mature sharks among the 108 test sharks. A change of \(b\) moves all sharks in the same way, which is one reason why \(b\) has the largest Fisher entry in the next section.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. After any fine-tuning run, keep a small test set from the old task and score it again. A drop of 10 points or more shows forgetting, and a model card that reports only the new task's score hides it.

How the figure was made

The curves are means of 20 networks, with a clarity input. They are for the network with four hidden units.

More questions

In the code's output the clear-water accuracy is 77.8% at step 25 and 80.6% at step 200. Has the network recovered the old water?

No. The difference is 3 sharks out of 108, within the noise of one network. Tag 9840 shows the loss: its chance of "mature" is still 0.79 against 0.18 at the start, so single predictions moved a long way.

Which weights does the old water need?

Guess first. You nudge one weight of the clear-water model by 1. Which nudge changes the model's predictions on clear-water sharks most: the weight \(w\) on length, the bias \(b\), or the weight \(c\) on the clarity reading?

The model is a logistic regression: the weighted sum \(z = w\,x + b + c\,v\) of the standardised length \(x\) and clarity reading \(v\) (the water's visibility) gives the chance of "mature", \(p = \sigma(z)\). The Fisher information is a table with one entry per pair of weights, and its diagonal \(F_{jj}\) has one entry per weight \(j\). \(F_{jj}\) measures how much the predictions change when only that weight is nudged. For a small nudge \(\delta\) the average change is about \(\tfrac12 F_{jj}\delta^2\).

  1. Set \(\delta = 1\) and choose \(w\), \(b\) and \(c\) in turn. The right plot shows the average KL divergence over the 160 made-up training sharks, in nats, which measures how far the predictions have moved (0 means no change).
  2. On the left, the dashed curve is the chance of "mature" before the nudge and the solid curve after it. Nudging \(c\) does not move the curve, because the clarity reading is about 0 in clear water.
  3. Choose \(b\) and drag \(\delta\) towards 0: the measured change (teal tile) comes close to the parabola \(\tfrac12 F\delta^2\) (navy tile).

Nudging the bias by 1 changes the predictions about 94 times more than nudging the clarity weight by 1, and for small nudges the change follows the parabola \(\tfrac12 F_{jj}\delta^2\).

How it works

Slopes for one shark. For one shark with label \(y\) (1 for mature, 0 for immature) the slope of the log loss for a weight is \(p-y\) times the input of that weight. This gives \((p-y)x\) for \(w\), \(p-y\) for \(b\), whose input is always 1, and \((p-y)v\) for \(c\). \(F_{jj}\) is the mean over the \(m\) training sharks of the squared slope \(\partial\ell_i/\partial\theta_j\), where \(\ell_i\) is the log loss of shark \(i\). A weight with large squared slopes has a large \(F_{jj}\), so a nudge of it changes the predictions more. For the bias, Tag 3305 (41.0 cm, mature) has \(p = 0.983\), so its squared slope is \((0.983-1)^2 = 0.00029\). Tag 9840 (30.7 cm, immature) has \(p = 0.105\), so \(p - y = -0.105\) and its squared slope is \(0.105^2 = 0.011\), which is 38 times larger.

Tag 330541.0 cm, mature, p = 0.983→(0.983 − 1)² = 0.00029squared slope of b|Tag 984030.7 cm, immature, p = 0.105→(0.105 − 0)² = 0.011squared slope of b=38×larger

\[ F_{jj} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\Big(\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \theta_j}\Big)^{2} \]

Common belief. The weights with the largest values are the ones the predictions depend on most.

Why it fails. In the clear-water model \(w = 5.18\) is larger than \(b = 2.94\). Yet \(F_{bb} = 0.065\) is about 2.6 times \(F_{ww} = 0.025\), so a small nudge of \(b\) changes the predictions more than the same nudge of \(w\).

Better account. How much a weight matters depends on its input and on how the predictions respond, and the Fisher diagonal measures that.

Quick quiz

A weight has \(F_{jj} = 0.06\). How much does the average KL divergence change for a nudge of 0.5?

\(\tfrac12 \times 0.06 \times 0.5^2 = 0.0075\) nats.

A shark has \(p = 0.5\) and \(y = 1\). How does its squared slope for \(b\) compare with Tag 9840's, 0.011?

\((0.5 - 1)^2 = 0.25\), which is about 23 times larger. In this model the sharks with \(p\) far from \(y\) dominate the Fisher diagonal: the 48 sharks with \(\lvert p-y\rvert > 0.1\) supply 99% of \(F_{bb}\).

Go deeper the idea, the estimate, checks, Python, limits about 7 min

The answer to the guess

The answer to the guess is the bias, or in these numbers about 0.06 for \(b\), 0.025 for \(w\) and 0.0007 for \(c\), as the readout shows. The clarity weight barely matters in clear water because its input is almost constant there.

The KL divergence

The KL divergence says how far one set of predicted probabilities has moved from another, in nats (0.7); 0 means no change.

The idea

For one input \(x\), the model assigns probabilities \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\) to the answers. Move the weights by a small \(\boldsymbol\delta\), and the probabilities change. The average change, measured by the KL divergence, is for small \(\boldsymbol\delta\) a quadratic: \(\mathrm{KL} \approx \tfrac12\,\boldsymbol\delta^\top F\,\boldsymbol\delta\). The matrix \(F\) is the Fisher information. Its entry \(F_{jj}\) answers: how much do predictions change per unit of weight \(j\)? Its off-diagonal entries say how a move in weight \(j\) and a move in weight \(k\) interact. The curves of the figure are this formula for one weight at a time.

The estimate

You do not need to move any weight to compute \(F_{jj}\). Differentiate the log probability. For one example, \(g_j = \partial \ln p_\theta(y\mid x) / \partial \theta_j\) says how fast the log probability of the answer changes with weight \(j\). It is the same slope the training loss uses, up to a sign. Averaging the square \(g_j^2\) over the examples gives \(F_{jj}\), the empirical Fisher diagonal. The squares make positive and negative slopes count in the same way. For the logistic model the slope has a simple form that you have met before (B4). It is \(g_j = (p - y)\,f_j\), where \(f_j\) is the input of weight \(j\) and \(f = (x, 1, v)\).

Which sharks matter

Over the 160 training sharks, the 48 whose error \(\lvert p-y\rvert\) exceeds 0.1 supply 99% of \(F_{bb}\). A likely reason why the Fisher marks the weights an old task needs is that it is built from the sharks the model finds hard, and for those sharks moving a weight is more likely to change the answer.

The same sharks for the length weight

The slope for \(w\) is \((p - y)\,x\), with \(x\) the standardised length. Tag 3305 has \(x = 0.216\), so its squared slope for \(w\) is \(0.00029 \times 0.216^2 = 0.000013\). Tag 9840 has \(x = -0.980\), so its squared slope is \(0.0111 \times 0.960 = 0.0107\). The factor \(x^2\) is why \(F_{ww}\) (0.025) is smaller than \(F_{bb}\) (0.065). A shark of average length has \(x\) near 0, so a nudge of \(w\) hardly moves its weighted sum, however unsure the model is about it.

Checking the parabola

Nudge \(b\) by 0.5. For Tag 9840 the weighted sum moves from \(-2.14\) to \(-1.64\), and the chance of "mature" from 0.105 to 0.163. The KL divergence, worked out without rounding, is 0.0134. The parabola \(\tfrac12\,p(1-p)\,\delta^2\) gives \(\tfrac12 \times 0.0943 \times 0.25 = 0.0118\), which is 12% lower. The gap shrinks with the nudge: for \(\delta = 0.1\) the two agree within 3%. For one shark and the bias, the Fisher entry is \(p(1-p)\) when the label is drawn from the model, which is the curvature of the log loss.

The full definition

\[ F_{jk} \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x}\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p_\theta(y\mid x)}\!\left[\frac{\partial \ln p_\theta(y\mid x)}{\partial\theta_j}\,\frac{\partial \ln p_\theta(y\mid x)}{\partial\theta_k}\right] \qquad\quad F_{jj} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\Big(\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \theta_j}\Big)^{2} \]

  • \(F_{jk}\) is the Fisher information matrix, one entry per pair of weights, and \(F_{jj}\) its diagonal. \(\theta_j\) is weight \(j\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}_x\) averages over the inputs (the old task's data). \(\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p_\theta}\) averages over answers that the model itself draws, not over the true labels.
  • The right-hand form is the estimate with the true labels: \(\ell_i\) is the loss of example \(i\) and \(m\) the number of examples (not Adam's \(m\)). It is called the empirical Fisher.

Why use the true labels?

For a model whose probabilities are well calibrated, the answers it draws match the true labels on average, and the two versions agree. For the logistic model \(\mathbb{E}\big[(p - y)^2\big] = p(1-p)\) when \(y\) is drawn with probability \(p\), which is the curvature of the loss. This is the identity used in B5, and the step that connects the Fisher information to the curvature of 0.6. In the network figures below the two versions of the diagonal have a rank correlation of 0.98.

Where it misleads

The full matrix has one entry per pair of weights. Our network has 25 weights and 625 entries. GPT-2 Small has 124 million weights and about \(1.5\times10^{16}\) entries, so EWC (the next section) stores only the diagonal. The diagonal ignores how weights tilt together (the valley of B5), and the directions along which the predictions change most are the eigenvectors of \(F\) with the largest eigenvalues (0.5). The empirical Fisher is also not the same as the curvature in general. Kunstner and others (2019) argue that it is an unreliable substitute for the true Fisher and for the curvature, and that updates built from it can be poor. The Fisher also shows what the trained model uses, which need not be what is true. With only 160 sharks, one hidden unit of the small network has a larger \(F\) for depth than for length (bar chart below). Depth has no information about maturity in the made-up table.

How many sharks are enough?

The estimate is an average, so it is noisy when built from few examples. Random subsets of the 160 training sharks were drawn, 200 times at the three sizes. With 20 sharks \(F_{bb}\) averages 0.065 and its spread across draws is 0.035, about half of its value. With 40 sharks the spread is 0.021, and with 80 it is 0.013, a fifth of the value. The mean stays near 0.065 in all three cases. In practice, use as many old-task examples as you can afford. Compare the estimates from two halves of the data to see whether the ranking of the weights is stable. The script below computes the three entries from all 160 sharks.

In Python

import json, numpy as np

rec = [r for r in json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"] if r["species"] == "spadenose"]
tr = np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(len(rec))[:160]                  # the 160 training sharks
L = np.array([rec[i]["length_cm"] for i in tr]); y = np.array([rec[i]["mature"] for i in tr], float)
x = (L - 39.138) / 8.614                                      # standardised length
v = np.random.RandomState(7).normal(0, 0.1, len(rec))[tr]       # clarity in clear water: 8 m, so 0 standardised, plus 0.4 m of noise
F = np.stack([x, np.ones(160), v], 1)                         # inputs of w, b, c
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

theta = np.zeros(3); ridge = np.array([1e-4, 1e-4, 40.0])     # c is held near 0 by a strong ridge, as in the figures
for _ in range(50):                                           # Newton steps for logistic regression
    p = sigmoid(F @ theta)
    g = F.T @ (p - y) / 160 + ridge * theta
    H = (F * (p * (1 - p))[:, None]).T @ F / 160 + np.diag(ridge)
    theta -= np.linalg.solve(H, g)

p = sigmoid(F @ theta)
slopes = (p - y)[:, None] * F                                 # one row of slopes per shark: (p - y) * input
fisher = (slopes ** 2).mean(0)                                # average squared slope = Fisher diagonal
print("weights w, b, c:", np.round(theta, 3))
print("Fisher diagonal F_w, F_b, F_c:", np.round(fisher, 4))
print("F_b / F_c = %.0f" % (fisher[1] / fisher[2]))
big = np.abs(p - y) > 0.1
print("sharks with |p - y| > 0.1: %d of 160, share of F_b: %.2f" % (big.sum(), (slopes[big, 1] ** 2).sum() / (slopes[:, 1] ** 2).sum()))
weights w, b, c: [5.182 2.938 0.   ]
Fisher diagonal F_w, F_b, F_c: [0.0253 0.0648 0.0007]
F_b / F_c = 95
sharks with |p - y| > 0.1: 48 of 160, share of F_b: 0.99

The three entries match the figure, and so does the share of the 48 uncertain sharks, 99%. The clarity entry is 95 times smaller than the bias entry, so the spring on \(c\) will be 95 times softer.

More questions

Why is the Fisher diagonal built from squared slopes and not plain slopes?

At a trained optimum the average plain slope is about 0, because positive and negative slopes cancel. The squared slope measures how large the slopes are, whatever their sign, and so how sensitive the predictions are.

Elastic weight consolidation: springs on the weights

Guess first. Fine-tuning on murky water now adds a penalty when a weight moves away from its old value, larger for weights with a larger Fisher diagonal. Will the network still learn the murky water?

Elastic weight consolidation (EWC) fine-tunes with the loss \(L = L_B + \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\sum_j F_{jj}(\theta_j - \theta^*_j)^2\). Here \(L_B\) is the loss on the new water and \(\theta^*\) the weights after the old water. \(F_{jj}\) is the old water's Fisher diagonal, which a person measures once at \(\theta^*\); \(\lambda\) is a strength that a person chooses. A term of the sum acts like a spring between weight \(j\) and its old value, with stiffness \(\lambda F_{jj}\). Weights that the old water's loss hardly depends on have soft springs, so they can still move.

  1. Press Play. The teal point leaves the old optimum (navy dot) and moves along the coral valley. The sand zigzags are the springs, thicker when stiffer. The stiff spring on \(b\) keeps \(b\) near 2.97.
  2. Drag \(\lambda\) to 300: the point stays nearer the old optimum, and murky-water accuracy falls to 60%. Drag it to 0: the point goes to the coral star, where plain fine-tuning ends.
  3. Back at \(\lambda = 30\), choose same springs on all weights, with the same total stiffness: murky-water accuracy is 43%.

At \(\lambda = 30\) the point moves \(c\) to \(-4.8\) and keeps \(b\) near 2.97, giving 86% in clear water and 84% in murky water, against 68% and 89% without springs.

How it works

Take \(\lambda = 30\). The old water's loss depends on \(b\) but hardly on \(c\): \(F_{bb} = 0.0648\) and \(F_{cc} = 0.00068\). So the spring on \(c\) is about 95 times softer. Moving a weight by \(\Delta\) adds \(\tfrac12 \times \text{stiffness} \times \Delta^2\) to the loss, the energy of a spring. This is about 64 for the plain move of \(b\) by 8.1 and 0.23 for the EWC move of \(c\) by 4.8. In murky water the standardised clarity reading is \(v = -1.5\), so \(b + c\,v = 2.97 + 4.8 \times 1.5 = 10.2\), close to the 11.0 that plain fine-tuning reaches with \(b\).

30 × 0.0648\(\lambda \times F\) for \(b\)=1.94stiffness of the \(b\) spring→½ × 1.94 × 8.1² ≈ 64plain move of \(b\) by 8.1|30 × 0.00068\(\lambda \times F\) for \(c\)=0.020stiffness of the \(c\) spring→½ × 0.020 × 4.8² = 0.23EWC move of \(c\) by 4.8
  1. The same method in the small network (made-up records, means of 20 networks). At \(\lambda = 30\) the solid curves end at 87% in clear water (coral) and 86% in murky water (teal). The dotted curves show plain fine-tuning ending at 73% and 86%.
  2. Choose no clarity reading: the solid curves end at 74% and 69%, against 68% and 87% for plain fine-tuning. Among the three values of \(\lambda\) on the slider, none keeps both accuracies above 80%.
  3. With a clarity reading again, choose Fisher springs, same springs and replay of 20 sharks (20 stored clear-water sharks mixed into the batches) in turn: the end points are 87% and 86%, 75% and 69%, and 85% and 85%. The Python code behind this figure, which the practice exercises build on, is in Go deeper.

Analogy. The weights are the knots of a net, the old values are pegs in the wall, and a spring joins a knot to its peg. Knots that the old water needs get stiff springs, and the others get slack ones.

Where it breaks. A spring's energy, \(\tfrac12 \times \text{stiffness} \times \Delta^2\), is a parabola in the stretch \(\Delta\). The old loss is close to a parabola only near \(\theta^*\), so the penalty can misjudge the cost of a large move. Two tasks that need the same weights to differ cannot both be served by one set of weights, as the no-clarity case shows for \(\lambda\) = 10, 30 and 100.

Quick quiz

How can EWC protect a model that no longer sees the old data?

The old data was used once, at the end of the old task, to measure \(F\) and store \(\theta^*\). After that the penalty needs only those two lists of numbers, not the sharks.

Two weights have \(F = 0.001\) and \(F = 0.1\). At \(\lambda = 30\), what does a move of 2 cost on their springs?

\(\tfrac12 \times 30 \times 0.001 \times 2^2 = 0.06\) and \(\tfrac12 \times 30 \times 0.1 \times 2^2 = 6.0\). The second move costs 100 times more, so the weight with the larger Fisher entry stays near its old value.

Go deeper derivation, Python, soft freezing, choosing lambda about 6 min

The answer to the guess

The answer to the guess is yes, when there is a free weight to learn through. In the old water the clarity reading is almost constant, so \(F_{cc}\) is almost 0 and the spring on \(c\) is slack. The stiff spring on \(b\) keeps the point on the old valley. With "same springs on all weights" (the same total stiffness) the spring on \(c\) resists what the new water needs, so the murky water is learned worse: 43% at \(\lambda=30\) against 84%.

Why this penalty

Kirkpatrick and colleagues (2017) derive EWC from Bayes' rule. After the old water the weights should stay where the old data makes them likely, and all we know about that is the old loss. Three steps turn this into the penalty. First, near its lowest point the old loss is a bowl. Its slope is 0 at \(\theta^*\), so a Taylor series (0.6) gives \(L_A(\theta) \approx L_A(\theta^*) + \tfrac12(\theta-\theta^*)^\top H\,(\theta-\theta^*)\), where \(H\) is the matrix of second derivatives. Second, when the model's probabilities are close to the truth, the Fisher information equals that curvature (the identity of the last section), so \(H \approx F\). In Bayesian terms the bowl is a Gaussian approximation to the information that the old data gives about the weights. Third, keep only the diagonal of \(F\). The new loss plus this bowl for the old task is the EWC loss. Moving a weight by \(\Delta\) costs \(\tfrac12\lambda F_{jj}\Delta^2\), the energy of a spring with stiffness \(\lambda F_{jj}\).

The penalty as an equation

\[ L(\theta) \;=\; L_B(\theta) \;+\; \frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{j} F_{jj}\,\big(\theta_j - \theta^{*}_{j}\big)^{2} \]

  • \(L_B\) is the loss on the new task and \(\theta^*\) the weights at the end of the old task. \(F_{jj}\) is the Fisher diagonal for the old task, measured at \(\theta^*\) and fixed during the new training.
  • \(\lambda\) is the strength, a number you choose. A new weight \(\theta_j\) that is far from \(\theta^*_j\) pays more when \(F_{jj}\) is large. At \(\lambda = 0\) this is plain fine-tuning.

The network figure

At \(\lambda = 30\) the network ends at 87% in clear water and 86% in murky water. Plain fine-tuning (dotted) ends at 73% and 86%. With no clarity reading, none of the values of \(\lambda\) tried gives both: 74% and 69% at \(\lambda=30\), against 68% and 87% for plain fine-tuning. Means of 20 networks. "Same springs" uses the mean of the Fisher diagonal for all weights, and replay mixes 20 stored clear-water sharks into the batches.

Between \(\lambda = 3\) and 100 the clear-water accuracy stays at 85 to 88% and the murky-water accuracy falls slowly from 85% to 84%. At 300 it falls to 79%. The no-reading case is the limit of the method. When both waters need the same weights in different ways (the weights \(w\) and \(b\) of the earlier picture), none of the springs tried gives both accuracies. EWC can choose a point on the trade-off, but here it does not remove the conflict.

In Python

def ewc(lam):                       # the penalty, in a few lines
    return lambda m: 0.5 * lam * sum(
        (f * (q - s) ** 2).sum()
        for f, q, s in zip(fisher, m.parameters(), star))

# fisher[k]: average squared slope of weight k over the old water's sharks
# star[k]:   the weight's value at the end of the old training
for name, lam in [("plain fine-tuning", 0), ("EWC, lambda = 30", 30)]:
    m = copy.deepcopy(net)
    fit(m, XB, 200, ewc(lam) if lam else None)
    print("%-24s: clear %.3f  murky %.3f" % (name, acc(m, XA), acc(m, XB)))

 [0.    0.    0.    0.   ]

The code prints one network, and the figure averages 20, so its numbers differ from the caption. Its Fisher table shows one more fact. Hidden units 3 and 4 are off for all clear-water sharks, so all weights in their rows have \(F = 0\) and the springs on them are slack. They are spare capacity, and EWC lets the new water use it. The set-up lines at the top of the script are in the notes at the end of the page.

Springs as a soft way of freezing

Instead of springs, you could freeze the weights that matter and train the rest. Four settings were tried in the three-weight model, trained on the 160 sharks and scored on the 108 test sharks, with \(\lambda = 30\) where springs are used. The accuracies are clear water first and murky water second.

  • Plain fine-tuning of \(b\) and \(c\): 68% and 89%.
  • Springs on \(b\) and \(c\), the EWC run: 86% and 84%.
  • Springs, but only \(b\) allowed to move: 89% and 37%. The stiff spring on \(b\) blocks the new water, and \(c\) cannot help.
  • No springs, \(b\) frozen, only \(c\) trained: 86% and 83%.

The last line is the point. Once you know that \(c\) is the free weight, plain training of \(c\) alone matches EWC. The Fisher diagonal finds that free weight for you, and a spring lets the other weights give a little if the new task needs it. In a network with millions of weights it is harder to find such a short list by hand, and the springs use the Fisher diagonal to rank the weights instead.

Choosing lambda

The network sweep gives a rule. The pairs below are clear-water and murky-water accuracy, means of 20 networks. At \(\lambda = 3\): 84.7% and 85.3%. At 10: 87.2% and 85.6%. At 30: 87.4% and 85.6%. At 100: 87.7% and 83.5%. At 300: 87.6% and 79.1%. Take the smallest \(\lambda\) whose old-water accuracy is within a point of the best, 87.7%. That is 10. Past it the old water gains at most half a point, and the new water loses up to 6.5 points. Here the sweep uses the test sharks to show the trade; in practice use validation sets of the waters.

Limits of the method

The Fisher is measured once, at the end of the old task. After several tasks you must keep one Fisher and one anchor per task, or merge them. The diagonal leaves out the tilt between weights.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Print the penalty next to the new loss at the start of fine-tuning. If the penalty is thousands of times the loss, the model cannot move and \(\lambda\) is too large. If it stays near 0, \(\lambda\) is too small to matter. A common heuristic is a \(\lambda\) that puts the penalty within a factor of ten of the loss after a few steps. In practice, \(\lambda\) is tuned like a learning rate, on a small grid. Published values vary by many orders of magnitude with the model and the scale of \(F\). In my primer the best \(\lambda\) was \(10^7\) at 1B and 3B parameters and higher at 8B.

More questions

A weight has \(F_{jj} = 0\) for the old task. What does EWC do to it?

The spring on it has stiffness 0, so it is as free as in plain fine-tuning. EWC leaves it to the new task.

Adam's v as a Fisher proxy

Guess first. Adam, an optimiser from the optimiser chapter, keeps a running average \(v\) of the squared slope of a weight, taken over mini-batches. The Fisher diagonal is also an average of squared slopes. How closely would the ranking of the weights by \(v\) after training match their ranking by the Fisher diagonal: not at all, roughly, or almost the same?

Adam's \(v\) can serve as a cheaper proxy for the Fisher diagonal \(F_{jj}\), with no extra pass over the old data when the saved \(v\) is available. At an optimum its size is about \(F_{jj}/B\) for batch size \(B\), so it should rank the weights like the Fisher diagonal, but on another scale.

  1. Coral bars are the Fisher diagonal and navy bars Adam's \(v\) after training, in a small network on made-up records. Teal bars are a rebuilt \(v\), measured again in 200 tiny steps at the finished weights when the saved \(v\) is missing. Hover over a bar for its value.
  2. Choose series scaled to sum to 1: the navy and teal bars are within a factor of 1.6 of the coral bar of the same weight. Their rank correlation with the Fisher diagonal is 0.98 (mean of 20 networks; 1 means the same order).

The series rank the 13 weights with \(F\) above 0 (of 25) almost alike, but \(v\) is 34 to 80 times smaller than \(F\) after training, and 14 to 25 times when rebuilt.

How it works

Take the weight from length to hidden unit 1 ("length to h1"). Its Fisher diagonal is \(F = 0.107\). With batches of \(B = 16\) in the 200 tiny steps, the rebuilt \(v\) should be about \(F/B = 0.107/16 = 0.0067\), and the measured value is 0.0065. The rule follows from \(\mathbb{E}[\bar g^2] = \tfrac1B\mathbb{E}[g^2] + (1-\tfrac1B)\,\mathbb{E}[g]^2\), where \(\mathbb{E}[\,]\) is the average over random draws from the training sharks and \(\bar g\) is the mean of \(B\) single-shark slopes \(g\). Here \(\mathbb{E}[g^2] = F\), and \(\mathbb{E}[g]\) is about 0 at an optimum. For the \(v\) kept from the original run, whose batches had 32 sharks, the rule gives \(0.107/32 = 0.0033\), and the measured value is 0.0026.

F = 0.107length to unit 1÷B = 16batch size of the rebuild=0.0067predicted vvs0.0065rebuilt v, measured

Common belief. Adam's \(v\) is the Fisher diagonal.

Why it fails. \(v\) averages squares of batch slopes, so it depends on the batch size \(B\). In the figure it is 34 to 80 times smaller than the Fisher diagonal. The rule gives \(F/B\) with \(B = 32\), so \(v\) is 1.1 to 2.5 times below it, for a reason that is not tested here.

Better account. \(v\) is a cheap proxy that ranks the weights almost as the Fisher diagonal does. Use it with its scale matched, for example by comparing penalties at the same total stiffness (matched strength).

Quick quiz

Why does \(v\) from batches of 32 come out many times smaller than the Fisher diagonal?

\(v\) averages the square of a batch mean. Near the optimum the mean slope is about 0, and averaging 32 example slopes shrinks the variance by about 32. The Fisher averages the squares of the single-example slopes. In the toy the measured gap is 34 to 80 times, a little wider than the batch size alone predicts.

Why does the rebuild take only tiny steps at the finished weights?

The aim is the sensitivity at the checkpoint. With a tiny learning rate (\(10^{-7}\) here) the weights barely move during the 200 steps. The slopes are then measured at the checkpoint, not at a point the run drifted to.

Go deeper steps, a second weight, Python, my project about 7 min

The answer to the guess

The answer to the guess is "almost the same ranking, different scale". Over all 13 weights the \(v\) kept from the original run is 34 to 80 times smaller than \(F\), 1.1 to 2.5 times the factor 32 of its batches. The \(1/B\) rule is a rough guide for a \(v\) saved from a run that was still moving.

The steps behind the factor

Square the batch mean and you get a double sum, \(\bar g^2 = \tfrac1{B^2}\sum_i\sum_k g_i g_k\). Take its average. The \(B\) terms with \(i = k\) all give \(\mathbb{E}[g^2]\). The \(B(B-1)\) terms with \(i \ne k\) pair two different sharks, which are independent, so they all give \(\mathbb{E}[g]^2\). Dividing by \(B^2\) leaves \(\tfrac1B\mathbb{E}[g^2] + (1-\tfrac1B)\mathbb{E}[g]^2\), the formula below. A second average gives the start-up correction. Adam begins with \(v = 0\) and updates it as \(v_t = \beta_2 v_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2)\bar g_t^{\,2}\). If the squared slope has the same average \(s\) at all steps, then \(v_t = (1-\beta_2^{\,t})\,s\). After 5 steps at \(\beta_2 = 0.95\) the factor is \(1 - 0.95^5 = 0.23\), so \(v\) shows only 23% of \(s\). After 200 steps the factor is 1.

A second weight

F = 0.284depth to unit 1÷16rebuilt, batch 16=0.0177predictedvs0.0154rebuilt v, measured|0.284 ÷ 32kept v, batch 32=0.0089predictedvs0.0035kept v, measured

A second weight shows the same two facts. For the weight from depth to unit 1, \(F = 0.284\). The rebuilt \(v\) is 0.0154 against the predicted 0.0177, which is 13% lower. The kept \(v\) is 0.0035 against 0.0089, which is 2.5 times lower. Over all 13 live weights, the rebuilt \(v\) is within 20% of \(F/16\) for 12 of them. The kept \(v\) is below \(F/32\) for all 13, by 1.1 to 2.5 times. Treat \(1/B\) as a guide to the order of magnitude for a kept \(v\), and measure \(v\) again when the scale matters.

The rebuild

Public checkpoints share a model's weights and usually not Adam's state, so \(v\) has to be measured again. The recipe in my optimizer-state work uses a Fisher run. Start from the checkpoint's weights with a fresh optimiser and take about 200 steps at a learning rate of \(10^{-7}\). The rate is so small that the weights barely move, which keeps all slopes measured at the checkpoint. Then correct the start-up bias, \(\hat v = v/(1-\beta_2^{t})\). In the toy, 200 steps at \(10^{-7}\) move no weight by more than \(4\times10^{-6}\). The \(\hat v\) has a rank correlation of 0.98 with the Fisher diagonal (mean of 20 toy networks).

Symbols

\[ \mathbb{E}\big[\bar g_j^{\,2}\big] \;=\; \frac{1}{B}\,\mathbb{E}\big[g_j^{2}\big] + \Big(1-\frac1B\Big)\big(\mathbb{E}[g_j]\big)^{2} \;\approx\; \frac{F_{jj}}{B} \qquad\quad \hat v_j = \frac{v_j}{1-\beta_2^{\,t}} \]

  • \(\bar g_j\) is the slope of weight \(j\) averaged over a batch of \(B\) examples, and \(g_j\) the slope for one example. \(F_{jj}\) is the Fisher diagonal (the average of \(g_j^2\)).
  • \(v_j\) is Adam's running average of \(\bar g_j^{\,2}\), \(\beta_2\) its memory factor and \(t\) the step count. The correction divides by \(1-\beta_2^t\), which is almost 1 after 200 steps at \(\beta_2 = 0.95\).

Matching the strength

Matched strength means comparing penalties at the same \(\lambda\,\lVert v\rVert_1\), where \(\lVert v\rVert_1\) is the sum of all entries of \(v\), so that scale does not decide the comparison. The rebuilt \(v\) is smaller than \(F\) by a roughly constant factor, so comparing penalties at one \(\lambda\) would be unfair. In the toy, the sum of the rebuilt \(v\) is 5.7% of the sum of \(F\) (mean of 20 networks). To give the rebuilt \(v\) the same total stiffness as the Fisher at \(\lambda = 30\), use \(\lambda' = 30/0.057 = 526\). The two penalties then have one overall strength and differ only in how they spread it over the weights, which is the comparison that matters.

Fisher against Adam's v

They are built differently, and the differences decide when one can replace the other.

  • The Fisher diagonal averages squared slopes of the log probability for single examples, with equal weight for all examples of the old task, at one fixed set of weights \(\theta^*\).
  • Adam's \(v\) is an exponential moving average of squared mini-batch slopes of the training loss. It weights the last \(1/(1-\beta_2)\) steps most, and the weights move between those steps.
  • So \(v\) is close to \(F/B\) when the weights are settled and the loss is the old task's. Otherwise it is a looser proxy, and penalties must be compared at matched strength.

In Python

def rebuilt_v(steps=200, lr=1e-7, batch=16):
    m = copy.deepcopy(net)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(0.9, 0.95))
    g = np.random.RandomState(2)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = tr[g.randint(0, 160, batch)]
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss_fn(m(XA[i]).squeeze(1), y[i]).backward()
        opt.step()
    st = opt.state_dict()["state"]
    v = torch.cat([st[k]["exp_avg_sq"].flatten() for k in range(4)])
    return v / (1 - 0.95 ** steps)         # undo the start-up bias

v = rebuilt_v()
F = torch.cat([f.flatten() for f in fisher]); live = F > 0
rank = lambda a: np.argsort(np.argsort(a))
r = np.corrcoef(rank(v[live].numpy()), rank(F[live].numpy()))[0, 1]
print("live weights:", int(live.sum()), "of", len(F))
print("rank correlation with the Fisher diagonal: %.2f" % r)
print("sum of v / sum of F: %.3f  (1/16 = %.3f)" % (v.sum() / F.sum(), 1 / 16))
live weights: 11 of 25
rank correlation with the Fisher diagonal: 0.94
sum of v / sum of F: 0.077  (1/16 = 0.062)

This is one network, the same one as in the EWC code. It has 11 live weights and a rank correlation of 0.94, and its \(F\) for length to unit 1 is 0.102. The figure uses another network with 13 live weights and quotes the mean over 20, so the numbers differ.

Bridge to my project. My manuscript (under review at TMLR) rebuilds AdamW's second moment from public data and uses it as a Fisher proxy for an EWC-style penalty, so that fine-tuning forgets less. My primer describes the recipe as a probe run of 10 steps at \(10^{-6}\) and a Fisher run of 200 steps at \(10^{-7}\). Both use the model's own \(\beta_2\) and \(\epsilon\), and \(\beta_2\) is 0.95 for all five models. Because the rebuilt \(v\) and the true \(v\) differ in scale, I compare penalties at matched strength \(\lambda\,\lVert v\rVert_1\), as defined under Matching the strength above. On Pythia 1B, I found that anchors with the same overall strength but equal or shuffled stiffness forgot 2.3 to 2.6 times more than the rebuilt \(v\). The equal springs of the EWC figure show the same pattern in the toy, whose numbers are made up and are not my results. See also the project page.

Where it breaks

The relation between \(v\) and the Fisher is loose. The value of \(v\) depends on the batch size (the factor \(1/B\) above). It also depends on the recent steps, a memory of about \(1/(1-\beta_2) = 20\) steps at 0.95, and on the weights having moved. A \(v\) saved from a moving model is stale for the checkpoint, which is one reason to measure it afresh, as in the Fisher run. Kunstner and others (2019) argue that the empirical Fisher, and so \(v\), is an unreliable substitute for curvature in general (B5 has the same warning). In the toy, 12 of the 25 weights have \(F = 0\) and \(v = 0\), so the agreement is easy for them. The result for the 13 live weights is the fair test. In practice, a proxy like this is a way to get a usable stiffness without storing the old data, and it still needs the matched-strength check.

More questions

The kept \(v\) in the second worked example was 2.5 times below \(F/32\). Give two reasons \(v\) can differ from \(F/B\).

First, \(v\) averages the last 20 or so steps of training, taken while the weights were still moving, and not the slopes at the finished checkpoint. Second, the formula drops the term \((1-1/B)\,\mathbb{E}[g]^2\), which adds to \(v\) wherever the mean slope is not 0.

Task after task: replay, springs and separate weights

Guess first. Four waters arrive one after another, and SharkCam must keep working in all of them. Which strategy keeps the most accuracy, and which needs the least memory: fine-tuning only, replaying stored sharks, EWC springs, or a separate copy of the network per water?

Continual learning means learning a sequence of tasks, ideally without forgetting the early ones. Fine-tuning only stores no extra data. Replay stores a few old sharks and mixes them into the new training. EWC (elastic weight consolidation) stores the weights and Fisher diagonal of an old water and adds a penalty. Separate weights means a frozen network per water, so the robot must know which water it is in. The forgetting of a water is its best accuracy since it was learned, minus its accuracy now.

  1. Choose fine-tune only and press Next water until dive 4 (a dive is one trip of the robot into a new water). A row gives the accuracy on the four waters after a dive.
  2. After dive 4 the three earlier waters are at 70%, 77% and 71%, against 88%, 87% and 87% when they were learned.
  3. Choose the other strategies in turn at dive 4 and compare the bars, which give the average over the four waters.

At dive 4, fine-tuning alone averages 76% over the four waters, replay and EWC 83%, separate weights 87% and joint training (one network trained on all four waters at once) 85%.

How it works

Read the grid by hand. The grid shows whole percents, and the values with one decimal are in the Python grid under Go deeper. After dive 4 the fine-tuning row reads 69.7, 77.3, 70.5 and 85.9%, so the average is \((69.7 + 77.3 + 70.5 + 85.9)/4 = 75.85\)%. The forgetting of the clear water is 88.1 − 69.7 = 18.4 points, because it had 88.1% after dive 1. Murky water had 86.9% after dive 2 and hazy water 87.4% after dive 3, so their forgetting is 9.6 and 16.9 points, and the mean forgetting is 15.0 points. Silt arrived last, so it has no earlier accuracy to lose yet.

88.1 − 69.7clear water: best minus now=18.4points|86.9 − 77.3murky water=9.6points|87.4 − 70.5hazy water=16.9points→15.0mean forgetting

Common belief. The best strategy is the one with the highest accuracy on the newest water.

Why it fails. After dive 4, fine-tuning only and separate weights are right for 86% on the newest water, more than EWC (79%). Yet fine-tuning only has the lowest average over the four waters, 76%, because it has forgotten the earlier waters.

Better account. Judge a strategy by the average over all waters seen so far and by the forgetting of the earlier waters.

Quick quiz

Which strategy forgets no old water by construction, and what does it need at test time?

Separate weights. A water's network is frozen after its dive, so its accuracy cannot change. At test time the robot must know which water it is in, to pick the network.

The sharks' photos are private and cannot be stored. Which of replay and EWC would you use, and what does it still need?

EWC. It stores only the weights and the Fisher diagonal of the old waters, and no photos. It still needs a tuned \(\lambda\). To check forgetting it would also need a small held-out set of old sharks, which the privacy rule would have to allow. EWC forgets less than plain fine-tuning (1.3 points against 15.0), but not zero.

Go deeper storage counts, combining methods, limits, Python about 5 min

The answer to the guess

Step through the dives with fine-tuning only. After dive 2 the murky water is at 87% and the clear water at 71%. After dive 3 the clear water is at 76%, the murky water at 66% and the hazy water at 87%. A new water usually lowers the earlier ones, though the clear water rose a little after dive 3. The answer to the guess depends on what you count. Separate weights win on accuracy (87%), because a water keeps its own network. They cost one network per water, and they need to know which water they are in when they run. The clarity reading could tell them, but a network per water does not scale to a thousand waters. Replay keeps 10 stored sharks per water and mixes them into training. It reaches 83% and has to store examples, which is a problem when the data is private or large. EWC stores the weights and \(F\) per water. It reaches 83% and needs no old data, and it needs a \(\lambda\) that you have tuned.

What the methods store

Count the numbers kept for the three old waters of the toy. Replay keeps 10 sharks per water, with 4 inputs and a label for a shark: \(10 \times 5 \times 3 = 150\) numbers. EWC keeps the weights and the Fisher diagonal of a water: \(2 \times 25 \times 3 = 150\). Separate weights keep one 25-weight network per water: 75. The counts are close here and grow differently. Replay grows with the examples you keep and their size, and a photo is far larger than five numbers. EWC adds two copies of the model per task. For a model of 1 billion weights stored in 2 bytes, that is 4 GB per task. Separate weights add one copy, 2 GB, unless the copy is a small adapter such as LoRA.

Combining the methods

The three families can be combined. Replay protects best the cases it replays, while a penalty protects more broadly. My primer notes this for language-model fine-tuning: replay of 5% FineWeb protected the text it replayed best, the anchor protected more broadly, and the two are complementary. A third group of methods grows the network, as the progressive networks of Rusu and others (2016) do with lateral connections from old to new columns. The "separate weights" row is the simplest version.

Where it misleads

The numbers are for four waters, a 25-weight network and a clarity reading that tells the waters apart. A sequence in the field has hundreds of tasks, no labels at the boundaries, and no clarity reading. Methods for that setting store experience (Rolnick and others, 2019, study replay without task boundaries in reinforcement learning) or detect the shift. The joint-training row, 85%, is not an upper limit here, since separate weights reach 87%. A likely reason is that one small network cannot fit all four waters as well as one network per water fits its own water. In practice, report the whole table instead of the last row alone. A model with a good average and one collapsed water is a different product from one with equal accuracy in all waters.
