More questions

Why is "average over the waters seen so far" a better summary than the accuracy on the newest water?

The newest water is learned reasonably well even by plain fine-tuning (86%), so it says little about what was lost. The average shows what was lost on the earlier ones.

Where test-time training fits

Guess first. The robot enters murky water and gets no labels. After about 20 frames (one camera image per shark), can it make its old rule work again without changing any weights?

In this chapter, continual learning updates a model between uses, with labels. Test-time training updates weights during use, without labels, on a loss built from the input. Test-time adaptation is the wider family, which changes something in the model during use, and its simplest member changes no weight. The robot keeps a running average (a mean updated one frame at a time) of the readings and of their spread. It standardises a new reading by subtracting the mean and dividing by the spread.

  1. Press Play. The left plot shows the share right in the last 20 frames. The coral line is the frozen (unchanged) clear-water rule, and the teal line is the same rule with the mean and spread re-estimated from the frames so far.
  2. Drag the slider to 20 and then to 108 frames (all the test sharks). The readout counts all frames so far.
  3. On the right, the teal running mean is within 1 cm of the water's true mean, 24.3 cm (dashed), from frame 6 on, far from the clear-water mean, 39.1 cm (dotted).

Re-estimating the mean and spread makes the rule right in 80% of the first 20 made-up frames and 87% of all 108, against 30% and 36% for the frozen rule.

How it works

Take Tag 3305, 41.0 cm. In clear water, with mean 39.14 cm and spread 8.61 cm, its standardised length is \((41.0 - 39.14)/8.61 = 0.216\). In murky water the camera reads \(0.62 \times 41.0 = 25.42\) cm, and the running mean and spread approach \(0.62 \times 39.14 = 24.27\) cm and \(0.62 \times 8.61 = 5.34\) cm. The shark then reads \((25.42 - 24.27)/5.34 = 0.215\), so the old weights see the clear-water input again. In general \((fL - f\mu)/(f\sigma) = (L - \mu)/\sigma\), so the factor \(f\) cancels.

25.42 − 24.27reading minus running mean, cm÷5.34running spread, cm=0.215input in murky water≈0.216input in clear water

The running statistics are estimates. After \(n\) frames the running mean is uncertain by about the spread divided by \(\sqrt n\): 2.4 cm after 5 frames, 1.2 cm after 20 and 0.6 cm after 80. So the mean is least certain in the first frames, a likely reason why they are worse.

Common belief. Standardising with running statistics always repairs a change in the water.

Why it fails. The repair assumes that the frames are a fair sample of the sharks. In the Python code under Go deeper, the 108 test sharks arrive smallest first, so the running mean falls too low. The adapting rule is then right for only 20% of the first 20 frames and 70% overall. In random order it is right for 87%.

Better account. The repair works when the change in the water is a rescaling and the frames come in a fair order. Check both before trusting it.

Quick quiz

Why does re-standardising with running statistics fix a pure rescaling of the readings?

Standardising turns \((fL - f\mu)/(f\sigma)\) into \((L-\mu)/\sigma\), so the factor \(f\) cancels. The old weights then see the same numbers as in the old water.

Name one thing that would stop this trick from working.

A shift that is not a rescaling of the inputs would stop it, for example one that changes how length relates to maturity. Frames in an unfair order, or a water with very few frames, would too, because the running mean is then off or still noisy.

Go deeper test-time training, my project, Python, drift about 5 min

The answer to the guess

The answer to the guess is yes, here. A rescaling of all the readings is undone by standardising with the water's own mean and spread. This is the simplest form of test-time adaptation. No weight changes, and no label is used, so what the model knew about the old water is not overwritten. It works here because this shift is a pure rescaling. Actual changes in light, colour and haze are not that tidy, so C3 adapts normalisation statistics and some weights of an image network, and tests when that helps.

Terms

Test-time adaptation (C3) changes something in the model while it is in use, from the unlabelled inputs it sees. Test-time training (C3) does this by updating weights on a self-supervised task built from the input. A running average (0.7) is a mean updated one frame at a time.

The size of the error

An error of 2.4 cm in the running mean is 0.45 of a spread (2.4/5.34).

Test-time training and the three modes

Test-time training goes one step further. Sun and others (2020) update the weights of the network on a test input by minimising a self-supervised loss. Such a loss needs no label, because its target is built from the input, for example the rotation that was applied to it. The updated weights then make the prediction. The three modes differ in when and with what they update:

  • Train once, deploy frozen. Weights never change. Cheap, and it can fail when the water changes.
  • Continual learning. Between deployments, with labelled data from the new water, using the methods of this chapter to avoid forgetting.
  • Test-time training. During deployment, with a self-supervised target, one input or one chunk at a time. It needs no labels, and it costs computation for all inputs.

Bridge to my project. In-Place Test-Time Training, a method from ByteDance Seed (Feng and others), treats the down projection of selected MLP blocks as fast weights. It updates them chunk by chunk as the model reads, with a target built from the input. Generation never pauses: an update happens in the step that completes a chunk. At MBZUAI, in Prof. Salman Khan's group, I am porting the method from text models to a Qwen vision-language model, so that it can adapt to an input after deployment. My motivation is the question of this chapter: recognising a shark when the water, light and animals change between dives. See the project page and its primer. D6 covers the long-context side.

How the figure was made

The 108 test sharks arrive in a fixed random order, in made-up murky water (factor 0.62). The frozen rule is the clear-water logistic regression.

Where it breaks

In the code below the 108 test sharks arrive smallest first, as when a school of small sharks swims past first. The frozen rule scores 36% either way. A slower update would react less to such a school and would adapt more slowly, which is the same trade as the memory \(\beta_2\) gives Adam's \(v\).

In Python

import json, numpy as np

rec = [r for r in json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"] if r["species"] == "spadenose"]
L = np.array([r["length_cm"] for r in rec]); y = np.array([r["mature"] for r in rec])
p = np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(len(rec)); te = p[160:]                # the 108 test sharks
mu0, sd0, w, b = 39.138, 8.614, 5.2892, 3.0008       # clear-water mean, spread and rule (z = w * x + b)

def run(order, f=0.62):
    """Frames arrive in the given order. Returns right-or-wrong for the frozen and the adapting rule."""
    reading = f * L[order]; label = y[order]
    frozen = ((w * (reading - mu0) / sd0 + b) > 0) == label
    adapt = np.zeros(len(order), bool)
    for t in range(len(order)):
        seen = reading[:t + 1]                                   # frames seen so far, this one included
        mu, sd = (seen.mean(), seen.std()) if t >= 4 else (mu0, sd0)      # keep the old scale for the first 4
        adapt[t] = ((w * (reading[t] - mu) / sd + b) > 0) == label[t]
    return frozen, adapt

order = te[np.random.RandomState(11).permutation(len(te))]
fz, ad = run(order)
print("random order    frozen %.2f  adapting %.2f  (first 20 frames: %.2f)" % (fz.mean(), ad.mean(), ad[:20].mean()))
small_first = te[np.argsort(L[te])]                              # a school of small sharks arrives first
fz, ad = run(small_first)
print("smallest first  frozen %.2f  adapting %.2f  (first 20 frames: %.2f)" % (fz.mean(), ad.mean(), ad[:20].mean()))
# standard error of the running mean after n frames, in the murky water (spread 0.62 * 8.614 = 5.34 cm)
for n in (5, 20, 80):
    print("after %2d frames the mean is uncertain by about %.1f cm" % (n, 0.62 * sd0 / np.sqrt(n)))
random order    frozen 0.36  adapting 0.87  (first 20 frames: 0.80)
smallest first  frozen 0.36  adapting 0.70  (first 20 frames: 0.20)
after  5 frames the mean is uncertain by about 2.4 cm
after 20 frames the mean is uncertain by about 1.2 cm
after 80 frames the mean is uncertain by about 0.6 cm

Where this fits with forgetting

A model that updates itself during use can drift. If all dives write into the same weights, the clear-water skill erodes in the way of the earlier figures. Test-time methods often limit what they change (a few fast weights, or only the statistics, as above), or reset after an input. In practice, ask three questions of any such method: what changes, what resets, and how you would notice damage. For SharkCam, the third is the small held-out set from the first water, scored after a dive.

More questions

After 5 frames the running mean is uncertain by about 2.4 cm. How uncertain is it after 4 times as many frames, and why?

About 1.2 cm. The uncertainty is the spread divided by \(\sqrt n\), and \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), so four times the frames halves it.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A weight penalty \(\omega\sum w^2\) is added to the loss, and the plain gradient step has learning rate \(\eta\). Show that one step multiplies a weight by \(1-2\eta\omega\) before the loss slope is applied. For \(\eta=0.1\) and \(\omega=0.05\), how many steps does it take for a weight with no loss slope to fall to half its size?

    Hint

    Differentiate \(\omega w^2\). Then solve \(0.99^t = 0.5\) with logarithms.

  2. theory A linear model predicts \(\hat y = w x\) with squared error. Add noise \(\varepsilon\) with mean 0 and variance \(s^2\) to the input, so the model sees \(x+\varepsilon\). Show that the expected squared error is the ordinary squared error plus \(s^2 w^2\). So input noise acts like a weight penalty. What is the penalty strength \(\omega\)?

    Hint

    Expand \((w(x+\varepsilon) - y)^2\) and take the average over \(\varepsilon\); the term linear in \(\varepsilon\) averages to 0.

  3. theory For logistic regression with probability \(p\) for the true answer, one example has slope \((p-y)f_j\) for weight \(j\). (a) Compute the squared slope of the bias for a shark with \(p=0.9\), \(y=1\) and for a shark with \(p=0.6\), \(y=1\). (b) A training set has 100 sharks like the first and 10 like the second. Which group has the larger share of \(F_{bb}\)?

    Hint

    The bias has \(f=1\). Multiply the squared slopes by the group sizes and compare.

  4. theory The old loss \(L_A\) has curvature \(k\) in one weight, with its minimum at \(\theta^*\). The new loss is \(L_B = \tfrac12 a(\theta-t)^2\), and the EWC penalty is \(\tfrac{\lambda}{2}k(\theta-\theta^*)^2\). Find the weight that minimises the sum, and show it lies between \(\theta^*\) and \(t\), closer to \(\theta^*\) when \(\lambda k\) is large compared with \(a\).

    Hint

    Set the derivative of the sum to 0. You should get a weighted average of \(\theta^*\) and \(t\) with weights \(\lambda k\) and \(a\).

Practice

  1. practice Use the code of the EWC section as a base. Train on the clear water, then fine-tune on the murky water with \(\lambda \in \{1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300\}\). Record the clear-water and murky-water accuracy for these, over five random seeds. Plot the two accuracies against one another. Where is the best trade-off?

    Hint

    Change the seed in torch.manual_seed and in fit. Average over seeds before plotting.

  2. practice Replace the Fisher diagonal in the EWC penalty by a list of ones scaled to the same sum. Fine-tune again at several \(\lambda\) and compare with the Fisher version at the same total stiffness. How much worse is the equal-springs run at its best \(\lambda\)?

  3. practice Compute the Fisher diagonal two ways for the clear-water network. First use the true labels. Then use labels drawn from the model's own probabilities (for two classes, weight the two label values by \(p\) and \(1-p\)). Compute the rank correlation of the two and the ratio of their sums.

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam will meet a new water once in a few weeks for years. Design the memory and testing plan. What do you store, and how often do you re-measure the Fisher? How do you notice that an old water has been forgotten? What would make you give up on one network and train a new one?

  2. open The "no clarity reading" case showed that EWC cannot serve two tasks that need the same weights to differ. Give two ways to break the conflict, one that changes the inputs and one that changes the network, and say what it costs.

  3. open A colleague proposes to measure the Fisher diagonal on the new data instead, to find out "which weights the new water needs", and to freeze the rest. What would this protect, what would it miss, and how would you test the proposal?

Come back later

(B5, B7) Adam's \(v\) for a weight is 0.004 after batches of 25. Roughly what is that weight's Fisher diagonal, and what do you need to assume?

About \(25 \times 0.004 = 0.1\), assuming the weight's mean slope is near 0 (the model is near an optimum) and \(v\) has settled. Dividing out the batch size is the step; the assumption fails for a model that is still moving.

(A4, B7) You fine-tune SharkCam on a new water and report 91% on the new test set. Name two other numbers you need before you call the run a success.

The accuracy on a held-out set from the old water, to catch forgetting. The accuracy of a lazy baseline on the new water (A4), to show the 91% means something. A third: a network trained from scratch on the same new data.

(B6, B7) Dropout, a weight penalty and early stopping all limit overfitting. Which of them changes the loss, which changes the network, and which changes only when training ends?

The weight penalty changes the loss. Dropout changes the network during training (B6). Early stopping changes only when training ends.

Notes for readers who want to rerun the figures. The catch records are the made-up table of data/sharks/catch.json (spadenose rows only). The four waters, the factors and the clarity readings are made-up choices described on this page. The networks are four-input, four-hidden-unit ReLU networks trained with Adam (\(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.95\)). The curves are means of 20 seeds, and the timeline of 10. The code blocks above are the core of the offline scripts, with the set-up lines below. The code leaves out the 0.4 m noise on the clarity readings that the figures use. Its clarity input is constant in clear water, so its Fisher for the clarity weights is 0 where the figure shows 0.0007, and its numbers differ a little.

import copy, json, numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn

rec = [r for r in json.load(open("catch.json"))["records"] if r["species"] == "spadenose"]
L = np.array([r["length_cm"] for r in rec]); G = np.array([r["girth_cm"] for r in rec])
D = np.array([r["depth_m"] for r in rec]); y = torch.tensor([float(r["mature"]) for r in rec])

def view(f, clarity):           # the readings in a water where the camera reads f times the true size
    X = np.stack([L * f, G * f, D, np.full(len(L), clarity)], 1)
    return torch.tensor((X - [39.14, 10.99, 22.35, 8.0]) / [8.61, 2.45, 9.45, 4.0], dtype=torch.float32)

p = np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(len(rec)); tr, te = p[:160], p[160:]
XA, XB = view(1.0, 8.0), view(0.62, 2.0)      # clear water, murky water (made-up factors)
loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()

def fit(net, X, steps, penalty=None, seed=1):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=0.02, betas=(0.9, 0.95))
    g = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = tr[g.randint(0, 160, 32)]
        opt.zero_grad(); loss = loss_fn(net(X[i]).squeeze(1), y[i])
        if penalty: loss = loss + penalty(net)
        loss.backward(); opt.step()

def acc(net, X): return ((net(X[te]).squeeze(1) > 0).float() == y[te]).float().mean().item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 1))
fit(net, XA, 300)                                         # learn the clear water
star = [q.detach().clone() for q in net.parameters()]     # theta*: the weights to protect
fisher = [torch.zeros_like(q) for q in net.parameters()]
for i in tr:                                              # F_jj: average squared slope
    net.zero_grad(); loss_fn(net(XA[i:i+1]).squeeze(1), y[i:i+1]).backward()
    for f, q in zip(fisher, net.parameters()): f += q.grad ** 2 / len(tr)
